```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
gsea <- read_csv(file.path(res, "gsea_hallmark.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(short = pathway |> str_remove("^HALLMARK_") |> str_replace_all("_", " ") |> str_to_sentence())
run <- read_csv(file.path(res, "running_score.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
tax <- read_csv(file.path(res, "tax_set_enrichment.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sprank <- read_csv(file.path(res, "species_ranking_outcome.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bal <- read_csv(file.path(res, "ranking_balance.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
balsum <- read_csv(file.path(res, "ranking_balance_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
generank <- read_csv(file.path(res, "gene_ranking_outcome.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
out <- gsea |> filter(ranking == "preterm vs term")
comm <- gsea |> filter(ranking == "anaerobe vs Lactobacillus")

# members of the top set, in ranked order, for the "gene set" slide
tnfa_members <- generank |> filter(in_top_set) |> arrange(rank) |> pull(symbol)

# set sizes on the two tables, for the scale slide
set_sizes <- bind_rows(
  out |> transmute(table = "Hallmark gene sets", size),
  tax |> filter(ranking == "genus") |> transmute(table = "genus sets", size)
) |> mutate(table = factor(table, c("Hallmark gene sets", "genus sets")))
```

## Yesterday you produced this {.center}

1,698 genes with an adjusted p-value below 0.05.

. . .

What is the finding?

## A gene list is hard to report {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- You cannot read 1,698 names
- You cannot put them in an abstract
- Two groups with the same data will hand you two different lists
:::

. . .

You need to say what the genes have **in common**.

## Cut-off tests and ranked tests

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 48%; font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.incremental}
- **Cut, then count.** Take your significant genes and a predefined set, and ask
  whether the overlap is bigger than chance (a hypergeometric test). It is simple,
  and it ignores every gene below your cutoff.
- **Rank, then look.** Order every gene you tested from most up to most down, and
  ask whether a set's members pile up at one end. This needs no cutoff. It is
  called gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).
:::

::: {.fragment}
We use GSEA, because with the first approach the answer depends on a threshold you
picked arbitrarily.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
cut <- sort(abs(generank$stat), decreasing = TRUE)[1698]
gr <- generank |> mutate(kept = abs(stat) >= cut)
p_rank <- ggplot(gr, aes(rank, stat)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-cut, cut), linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = kept), size = 0.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[["orange"]], `FALSE` = pal[["grey"]])) +
  annotate("text", x = nrow(gr) * 0.5, y = cut + 0.5, label = "cutoff",
           colour = "grey35", size = 4.5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "test statistic",
       title = "All 13,738 genes, ranked",
       subtitle = "Orange: kept by a cutoff. Grey: ignored by it.") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())
p_rug <- ggplot(filter(gr, in_top_set), aes(rank)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = rank, y = 0, yend = 1), colour = pal[["navy"]], alpha = 0.5) +
  xlim(1, nrow(gr)) +
  labs(x = "rank of the gene", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Where the members of one gene set fall") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
p_rank / p_rug + plot_layout(heights = c(3, 1))
```
:::
::::

## A gene set is a named list

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Someone curated it, from papers or experiments.

::: {.fragment}
We use the **Hallmark** collection: 50 sets of about 200 genes, one for each broad
biological program.
:::

::: {.fragment}
`HALLMARK_INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE`<br>
`HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB`<br>
`HALLMARK_INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE`
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; line-height: 1.5;"}
The first 40 of the `r length(tnfa_members)` `HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB`
genes in our table:

`r paste(head(tnfa_members, 40), collapse = " ")`
:::
:::
::::

## Rank by the test statistic

```{r}
#| eval: false
# res is your DESeq2 result table
stat <- res$stat
names(stat) <- rownames(res)
stat <- stat[!is.na(stat)]
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 55%; font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.incremental}
- The p-value has no sign, so A and B look identical.
- The fold change alone puts noisy gene C at the top.
- The statistic is the fold change divided by its standard error, so it carries
  both size and confidence.
:::
:::

::: {.column style="width: 45%; font-size: 0.7em;"}
| gene | log2 FC | std. error | p-value | statistic |
|:-----|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| A | +3.0 | 0.5 | 2e-9 | +6.0 |
| B | -3.0 | 0.5 | 2e-9 | -6.0 |
| C | +6.0 | 4.0 | 0.13 | +1.5 |

: Toy numbers
:::
::::

## Walk down the list and keep score

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
set.seed(1)
curve <- run |> filter(rank %% 7 == 0 | hit)
hits <- run |> filter(hit)
peak <- run$rank[which.max(run$running)]

p_top <- ggplot(curve, aes(rank, running)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "running score",
       title = "HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB, genes ranked from preterm-high to term-high") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())
p_bot <- ggplot(hits, aes(rank, y = 1)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = rank, y = 0, yend = 1), colour = pal[["navy"]], alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "rank of the gene", y = NULL) +
  xlim(1, max(run$rank)) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
p_top / p_bot + plot_layout(heights = c(3, 1))
```

Each tick is a set member. The score climbs at each hit and drifts down between
them.

## The number you report

The highest point the score reaches is the enrichment score. Shuffle the gene
labels many times to find out how surprising that peak is.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(fgsea)
library(msigdbr)

hallmark <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
sets <- split(hallmark$ensembl_gene, hallmark$gs_name)

fgsea(sets, stat, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500)
```

. . .

`NES` is the peak, normalised so sets of different sizes are comparable. Its sign
tells you which end of the ranking the set sits at.

## Preterm versus term

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5.4
out |> slice_min(padj, n = 12) |>
  mutate(short = fct_reorder(short, NES)) |>
  ggplot(aes(NES, short, fill = NES > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[["orange"]], `FALSE` = pal[["navy"]]),
                    labels = c("higher in term", "higher in preterm")) +
  labs(x = "normalised enrichment score", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Reading the top sets

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
out |> slice_min(padj, n = 6) |>
  transmute(set = short, size, NES = round(NES, 2), padj = format(padj, digits = 2)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```
:::

. . .

Inflammatory signalling, tumour necrosis factor, interferon and complement are
all shifted up in the people who delivered early.

. . .

You could put that sentence in an abstract, and it comes from the same 13,738
statistics that gave you the list of 1,698 genes.

## Now try the community contrast

Run the same analysis on yesterday's other contrast, anaerobe versus
Lactobacillus.

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
comm |> slice_min(padj, n = 6) |>
  transmute(set = short, size, NES = round(NES, 2), padj = format(padj, digits = 2)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```
:::

. . .

`r sum(comm$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` of 50 sets are significant, and
`r sum(comm$padj < 0.05 & comm$NES < 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of those point the same
way. Does that look like biology to you?

## Checking that the statistics are centred

Is the distribution of test statistics centred?

```{r}
#| echo: false
balsum |>
  transmute(ranking,
            `share of all genes positive` = scales::percent(share_positive_all, 0.1)) |>
  kable(align = "lr")
```

. . .

Both are near half, so by this check both rankings look fine.

. . .

The check is wrong, because GSEA does not weight genes equally. It weights each
gene by the size of its statistic.

## Look at the strong effects only

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(bal, aes(min_abs_stat, share_positive, colour = ranking)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`preterm vs term` = pal[["navy"]],
                                 `anaerobe vs Lactobacillus` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  labs(x = "keep only genes with |statistic| at least this large",
       y = "share of those genes that are positive", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Share positive at three levels

```{r}
#| echo: false
balsum |>
  transmute(ranking,
            `all genes` = scales::percent(share_positive_all, 0.1),
            `significant genes` = scales::percent(share_positive_significant, 0.1),
            `500 strongest` = scales::percent(share_positive_top500, 0.1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

::: {.incremental}
- Outcome: balanced at every level, so nothing pushes the sets one way.
- Community: balanced overall, but only
  `r scales::percent(balsum$share_positive_top500[balsum$ranking == "anaerobe vs Lactobacillus"], 0.1)`
  of the 500 strongest effects are positive.
:::

. . .

Every large gene set will be dragged toward the Lactobacillus end.

## The sets follow the tail

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  ranking = c("preterm vs term", "anaerobe vs Lactobacillus"),
  `significant sets` = c(sum(out$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), sum(comm$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)),
  `pointing one way` = c(
    max(sum(out$padj < 0.05 & out$NES > 0, na.rm = TRUE), sum(out$padj < 0.05 & out$NES < 0, na.rm = TRUE)),
    max(sum(comm$padj < 0.05 & comm$NES > 0, na.rm = TRUE), sum(comm$padj < 0.05 & comm$NES < 0, na.rm = TRUE)))
) |> kable(align = "lrr")
```

::: {.incremental}
- Outcome: the strong effects are balanced, and the sets still agree with each
  other. Here the agreement comes from the biology.
- Community: the strong effects nearly all point one way, and so do the sets.
  The lopsided ranking alone would produce that.
:::

## The individual genes still stand

The individual genes from the community contrast are still real. Mucins and
filaggrin were up in Lactobacillus-dominant samples by a factor of eight, with
adjusted p-values near ten to the minus eighteen.

. . .

The imbalance undermines the **set-level** claim, that a named program is
coordinately shifted. Large generic sets drift along with a lopsided list, so the
gene-level and set-level claims need separate checks.

## Check the tail every time {.center}

Before you believe an enrichment, sort your genes by the size of their effect
and look at the top few hundred.

. . .

If those nearly all point one way, every large set will come out enriched that
way, and the method will give you a very small p-value for it.

. . .

Our community ranking was centred overall and still failed this check.

## Limits of any gene set collection

::: {.incremental}
- Sets overlap. TNFA signalling and inflammatory response share many genes, so
  their p-values are not independent and you cannot count them as separate
  findings.
- People curated them, mostly from experiments in cell lines and mostly not from
  cervical tissue.
- If nobody has curated a set for the biology you study, enrichment cannot find
  it.
:::

## The same idea, on bacteria {.center}

A gene set is a label that groups features.

. . .

Species already carry labels that group them: **genus** and **family**.

## Rank species, test taxonomy

```{r}
#| eval: false
# the same fgsea call; only the sets changed
genus_sets <- split(species_results$feature, species_results$Genus)
fgsea(genus_sets, species_stat, minSize = 2, maxSize = 50)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 48%; font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
tax |> filter(ranking == "genus") |> slice_min(padj, n = 5) |>
  transmute(genus = pathway, size, NES = round(NES, 2), padj = format(padj, digits = 2)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.8
sp <- sprank |>
  mutate(group = case_when(Genus == "Gardnerella" ~ "Gardnerella",
                           Genus == "Prevotella" ~ "Prevotella",
                           TRUE ~ "other genera"),
         group = factor(group, c("Gardnerella", "Prevotella", "other genera")))
ggplot(sp, aes(rank, stat, colour = group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(data = filter(sp, group == "other genera"), size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = filter(sp, group != "other genera"), size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Gardnerella = pal[["orange"]],
                                 Prevotella = pal[["navy"]],
                                 `other genera` = pal[["grey"]]),
                     breaks = c("Gardnerella", "Prevotella", "other genera")) +
  labs(x = "rank of the species (preterm-high on the left)",
       y = "test statistic", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.text = element_text(face = "italic"))
```
:::
::::

*Gardnerella* comes out: two of its three species rank 1st and 4th toward preterm, which is enough for a three-member set.

## Set sizes on the two tables

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 45%; font-size: 0.8em;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  ` ` = c("features ranked", "sets tested", "typical set size", "sets significant"),
  genes = c("13,738", "50", "about 190", as.character(sum(out$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))),
  species = c(as.character(nrow(sprank)), as.character(sum(tax$ranking == "genus")),
              "2 to 12", as.character(sum(tax$padj < 0.05 & tax$ranking == "genus", na.rm = TRUE)))
) |> kable(align = "lrr")
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(set_sizes, aes(size, table, colour = table)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, width = 0, size = 3, alpha = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Hallmark gene sets` = pal[["orange"]],
                                 `genus sets` = pal[["teal"]])) +
  labs(x = "features in the set (log scale)", y = NULL)
```
:::
::::

. . .

Set-level analysis pays off when you have thousands of features and hundreds of
curated groups. With 53 species in ten genera, you are better off reading the
species list.

## Choosing a method for your table {.center}

The code was identical on genes and on species, but it only told us something new
about the genes.

. . .

Pick the method for how many features your table has and how they group, rather
than for whether it came from RNA-seq or 16S.
